Apodemus argenteus, the small Japanese field mouse, is a diminutive murid rodent widely distributed across the Japanese archipelago, where it inhabits forested montane and lowland habitats. Neonates emerge into the world at a remarkably modest mass of 1.4 grams [Wwb = 1.4 grams], a value that aligns closely with the altricial developmental strategy typical of small-bodied Apodemus species. This early life history strategy, featuring a very low neonatal mass of 1.4 grams [Wwb = 1.4 grams] and a brief in utero phase, is typical of species that rely on high fecundity to offset substantial juvenile mortality in unpredictable forest environments. The gestating female maintains an internal body temperature of approximately 37.5 °C [T = approximately 37.5 °C] and experiences a gestation period of 27.5 days [tg = 27.5 days]. The comparatively short gestational duration reflects the trade-off between producing a large litter and the limited maternal energetic capacity available for extended foetal development in such a small mammal. Fully developed pups are born hairless and entirely dependent on maternal care, and their rapid postnatal growth trajectory is made possible by the nutritious milk provided during the intensive suckling stage that follows immediately after parturition.

Reproductive output in this species follows a markedly slow annual pattern compared to many other small rodents. Captive records and field observations indicate that females produce only a single litter per year [F_R_i = single litter per year], a low frequency that sets Apodemus argenteus apart from its congener Apodemus speciosus, which often gives birth to two or three litters annually. This constrained annual recruitment rate, tied to a single yearly breeding event [F_R_i = single yearly breeding event] and a moderate litter size, appears linked to the seasonal abundance of seeds and invertebrates in temperate deciduous forests. Such a pattern of infrequent reproduction contrasts sharply with the prodigious reproductive output observed in many voles and mice of the subfamily Arvicolinae, which can produce several litters over a single breeding season under favorable conditions.

Weaning marks a critical developmental transition for the altricial pups, who must shift from complete nutritional dependence on maternal milk to independent foraging on solid foods. The time since birth at weaning is generally reported as 21 days [tx = 21 days], though some field studies note an extended range of 28 to 30 days since birth [tx = 28 to 30 days since birth] depending on local resource availability and maternal condition, all measured at the standard body temperature of 37.9 °C [T = 37.9 °C]. This relatively brief nursing period is characteristic of small murids and reflects the energetic imperative for females to minimize the inter-birth interval, particularly in a species constrained to a single annual litter [F_R_i = single annual litter]. The suckling juvenile phase places intense energetic demands on the lactating female, who must ingest sufficient calories to produce milk while simultaneously maintaining her own body condition for post-weaning survival. Once weaned, the young mice disperse into the surrounding understory, where they must rapidly acquire the foraging skills necessary to locate seeds, fruits, and arthropods in the complex forest floor environment. Successful weaning is therefore a pivotal event that determines the survival trajectory of the cohort within the challenging temperate woodland ecosystem.

The developmental schedule following weaning proceeds through a distinct juvenile and sub-adult phase before reproductive competence is attained. Puberty, as defined by the onset of gametogenesis and the first appearance of mature spermatozoa in males and ovarian follicles in females, occurs at 61 days after birth [tp = 61 days after birth], measured at the standard active body temperature of 37.9 °C [T = 37.9 °C]. This relatively protracted pre-reproductive interval, spanning approximately two months, allows young individuals to complete a substantial portion of somatic growth before investing energy in reproduction. The final adult body size, or asymptotic mass, reaches an ultimate wet weight of 13 grams [Wwi = 13 grams], a value that represents a nearly tenfold increase over the neonatal mass of 1.4 grams [Wwb = 1.4 grams]. This significant growth trajectory from a birth weight of 1.4 grams [Wwb = 1.4 grams] to an adult mass of 13 grams [Wwi = 13 grams] underscores the importance of the post-weaning foraging period, during which juveniles must accumulate sufficient protein and lipid reserves to support both metabolic demands and future reproductive effort. The species' comparatively small ultimate body size is consistent with its ecological niche as a forest-floor granivore and insectivore, where maneuverability among leaf litter and woody debris confers a selective advantage over larger-bodied competitors.

Lifespan in the small Japanese field mouse is remarkably extended relative to its diminutive body size, with maximum recorded longevity reaching 5 years [am = 5 years] under controlled captive conditions at a stable body temperature of 37.9 °C [T = 37.9 °C]. This lifespan is unusually long for a rodent weighing only 13 grams [Wwi = 13 grams], as most similarly sized murids seldom exceed two to three years in captivity, let alone in the wild. The survival pattern is characterized by a slow life-history pace, with the single annual litter and delayed puberty at 61 days after birth [tp = 61 days after birth] contributing to an extended reproductive window that can span multiple breeding seasons at a temperature of 37.9 °C [T = 37.9 °C]. This strategy contrasts with that of many sympatric rodents, such as the large Japanese field mouse, which exhibit faster maturation and higher annual fecundity but shorter overall lifespans.
